patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged altered consciousness, EEG shows bilateral frontal activity, isoniazid exposure discovered after admission — resistant to benzodiazepines
patient.history_present_illness: A 31-year-old White female pharmacy technician was brought to the emergency department after her roommate found her convulsing. EMS reports she was in generalized status epilepticus — continuous tonic-clonic activity for at least 8 minutes before EMS arrived, continuing on arrival. She was given IV lorazepam 4 mg with no response. Another 4 mg lorazepam was given with no response. She was intubated in the field and given IV fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg PE with continued seizure activity (unresponsive). She has no prior history of epilepsy. She has no known medical conditions. Her roommate found no medications in the apartment initially. She is currently on levetiracetam drip started by ED as third-line agent. Seizures have not fully stopped — intermittent clinical movements persist. Critical history discovered AFTER admission (45 minutes in): a colleague at the pharmacy calls and reports the patient had accidentally ingested a large amount of isoniazid (INH) — she was preparing a multi-dose vial and accidentally consumed the powder (approximately 10-15 grams) after a chemical spill incident at work earlier today. The colleague only just learned what had happened. Now the clinical picture suddenly makes sense: BENZODIAZEPINE-RESISTANT SE from isoniazid toxicity.

output.proposed: isoniazid (INH) 10-15 g accidental ingestion + IV pyridoxine 5 g antidote
interactions: Isoniazid + benzodiazepines: benzodiazepines require synaptic GABA to work; INH irreversibly inactivates pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP) — the cofactor for GABA synthesis — causing GABA depletion; explains complete benzodiazepine resistance in INH-induced SE.
Fosphenytoin/phenytoin + INH SE: fosphenytoin targets voltage-gated sodium channels — INH SE is GABA-depletion mediated, not sodium channel mediated; fosphenytoin is ineffective; do not use.
contraindications: Fosphenytoin and phenytoin: ineffective for INH-induced SE (wrong mechanism); do not use.
Succinylcholine: contraindicated if pseudocholinesterase inhibition is also suspected; use rocuronium.
warnings: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 5 g IV is the specific antidote: 1 g pyridoxine per gram of INH ingested; give 5 g empirically if amount unknown; administer over 30-60 minutes; seizures typically stop within 20-60 minutes.
After pyridoxine restores GABA synthesis, benzodiazepines become effective as adjunctive agents.

results.title: Isoniazid toxicity and treatment with pyridoxine
results.key_finding: INH SE is benzodiazepine-resistant because INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate, preventing GABA synthesis. Pyridoxine is the specific antidote: 1g IV per gram of INH ingested; if amount unknown, give 5g IV empirically. Fosphenytoin is ineffective. After pyridoxine, benzodiazepines become effective once GABA is restored. Prognosis excellent with early pyridoxine administration.

output.summary: Isoniazid toxicity depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP), the cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase; without PLP, GABA synthesis is impaired, rendering benzodiazepine receptor agonists ineffective. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is the specific antidote: 1 g IV per gram of INH ingested; 5 g IV empirically when the ingested dose is unknown. Seizures typically cease within 20–60 minutes of adequate pyridoxine. Fosphenytoin has no mechanistic efficacy in INH-induced SE. Standard urine drug screens do not detect isoniazid; serum INH levels require a reference laboratory but treatment should not await results.

contraindicated_actions: Fosphenytoin or phenytoin for INH SE — sodium channel blockade has no effect on GABA-depletion mechanism; will fail
Delaying pyridoxine administration for confirmatory INH level — treat empirically based on history; INH level is confirmatory, not prerequisite
Stopping at benzodiazepine escalation without considering toxic antidote — benzodiazepine refractoriness in young healthy patient signals specific toxin
key_reasoning_points: INH toxicity mechanism: INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP), the cofactor for GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase); without PLP, GABA synthesis stops; benzodiazepines require GABA at the receptor to work — benzodiazepine resistance = pathognomonic clue for GABA-depletion toxidrome

Benzodiazepine-refractory SE in young healthy patient is the KEY clinical clue — this pattern demands consideration of specific toxic antidote (INH → pyridoxine; organophosphate → atropine + pralidoxime; TCA → sodium bicarbonate)
Standard urine drug screens do NOT detect isoniazid — serum INH level requires reference lab; clinical history + pyridoxine depletion is sufficient to treat empirically

Fosphenytoin fails in INH SE — sodium channel mechanism is irrelevant to GABA-depletion pathophysiology; this is a critical clinical error in the case (fosphenytoin was given and failed, confirming INH etiology)
Pyridoxine dosing: 1g IV per 1g INH ingested (estimated); if amount unknown, 5g IV empirically; seizures stop within 20-60 minutes of adequate pyridoxine

metadata.pitfalls: Using fosphenytoin/phenytoin for INH SE; escalating benzodiazepines without antidote; not considering toxic etiology for benzodiazepine-resistant SE in healthy patient
metadata.clinical_pearl: Benzodiazepine-resistant SE in young healthy patient = toxic antidote SE. INH depletes GABA → pyridoxine 5g IV is the antidote. Standard UDS misses INH. Fosphenytoin will fail. Pyridoxine works in 20-45 minutes.
